Criterion A: Knowing and understanding:
# Criterion A: Knowing and understanding
## What it assesses
Criterion A: Knowing and understanding assesses knowledge of physical and health education. You explain physical and health education factual, procedural and conceptual knowledge; apply it to analyse issues and solve problems in familiar and unfamiliar situations; and apply physical and health terminology effectively.

## How to do well
Learn key terms such as the components of fitness and principles of training. Apply them to specific sports and scenarios with examples.

## How it is assessed
Each MYP criterion is marked from 0 to 8 using level descriptors, which describe what work looks like at each band. Command terms such as outline, explain, analyse and evaluate show the depth required. Teachers judge the best fit across the strands of the criterion.

## Key terms
Factual knowledge: facts such as rules and definitions
Procedural knowledge: knowing how to do something
Conceptual knowledge: understanding big ideas and links
Level descriptor: a description of what work looks like at each band
Command term: a word that shows the depth of answer required
Criterion B: Planning for performance:
# Criterion B: Planning for performance
## What it assesses
Criterion B: Planning for performance assesses how you design and analyse plans. You design, explain and justify plans to improve physical performance and health, and analyse and evaluate the effectiveness of a plan based on the outcome.

## How to do well
Set SMART goals. Use training principles such as overload and specificity. Explain why each activity is included and how you will measure progress.

## How it is assessed
Each MYP criterion is marked from 0 to 8 using level descriptors, which describe what work looks like at each band. Command terms such as outline, explain, analyse and evaluate show the depth required. Teachers judge the best fit across the strands of the criterion.

## Key terms
SMART goal: a specific, measurable, achievable, relevant, time-bound goal
Training plan: a planned programme of exercise
Outcome: the result of following a plan

Command term: a word that shows the depth of answer required

# Criterion C: Applying and performing
## What it assesses
Criterion C: Applying and performing assesses practical performance. You demonstrate and apply a range of skills and techniques effectively; demonstrate and apply a range of strategies and movement concepts; and analyse and apply information to perform effectively.

## How to do well
Practise skills until they are consistent. Use tactics suited to the situation. Adapt to opponents and conditions during play.

## How it is assessed
Each MYP criterion is marked from 0 to 8 using level descriptors, which describe what work looks like at each band. Command terms such as outline, explain, analyse and evaluate show the depth required. Teachers judge the best fit across the strands of the criterion.

## Key terms
Skill: a learned ability to perform a movement
Strategy: an overall plan for performance
Movement concept: an idea about how the body moves, such as space or effort

# Criterion D: Reflecting and improving performance
## What it assesses
Criterion D: Reflecting and improving performance assesses reflection and interpersonal skills. You explain and demonstrate strategies that enhance interpersonal skills; develop goals and apply strategies to enhance performance; and analyse and evaluate performance.

## How to do well
Reflect on performance with evidence such as videos, data or feedback. Identify strengths and weaknesses. Set new goals and explain strategies to reach them. Show respect, teamwork and communication.

Fitness and training principles:
# Fitness and training principles
## The topic
Health-related components of fitness are cardiovascular endurance, muscular strength, muscular endurance, flexibility and body composition. Skill-related components are agility, balance, coordination, power, reaction time and speed. Training principles include specificity, progression, overload (frequency, intensity, time and type, FITT), reversibility and recovery. Training methods include continuous, interval, circuit, fartlek and weight training. A warm-up raises heart rate and prepares muscles; a cool-down helps recovery.

## Key terms
Cardiovascular endurance: the ability of the heart and lungs to supply oxygen during exercise
Overload: working harder than usual to improve fitness
Specificity: training matched to the activity
Interval training: alternating work and rest periods
FITT principle: frequency, intensity, time and type
Health and nutrition:
# Health and nutrition
## The topic
A balanced diet contains carbohydrates, proteins, fats, vitamins, minerals, fibre and water in the right amounts. Carbohydrates are the main energy source; proteins build and repair muscle; fats store energy. Hydration is having enough water in the body. Sleep, mental health and avoiding drugs and alcohol support well-being. Energy balance is when energy intake equals energy used.

## Key terms
Balanced diet: a diet with all nutrients in the right amounts
Carbohydrate: the body’s main energy source
Protein: a nutrient that builds and repairs muscle
Hydration: having enough water in the body
Energy balance: energy intake equal to energy used
Skills and tactics:
# Skills and tactics
## The topic
A skill is a learned action performed with control. Open skills are affected by the environment, such as passing in football; closed skills are not, such as a free throw. Tactics are plans used in a game to beat opponents, such as zone defence or a fast break. Strategies are overall game plans. Feedback can be intrinsic (from the performer) or extrinsic (from others).

## Key terms
Open skill: a skill affected by the environment
Closed skill: a skill not affected by the environment
Tactic: a plan used in a game to beat opponents
Intrinsic feedback: feedback from the performer’s own senses
Extrinsic feedback: feedback from others such as a coach
